    "description": "## Current behavior\n\nSessions in `Projects/ddx/.ddx/agent-logs/sessions.jsonl` against thinking-mode local models (qwen3.5-27b, google/gemma-4-31b) abort with:\n\n```\nagent: agent: reasoning stall: model produced only reasoning tokens past stall timeout\n```\n\nThis is a useful detection — without it the agent would hang forever or burn output tokens. But the failure surface is a flat error string, so:\n\n- Cannot count \"stall rate\" as a metric across runs/models/prompts.\n- Cannot debug what the model was reasoning about when it stalled — the reasoning content is dropped.\n- Cannot tune the stall timeout per-model without touching code.\n\n## Proposed enhancements\n\n1. **Structured error code.** Define `REASONING_STALL` (or similar) in the agent error catalog so callers can match programmatically.\n2. **Capture last N reasoning tokens** (default ~500) in the error context. For local models this is just whatever the streaming buffer holds at stall time. Users debugging a stall need to see what the model was reasoning about.\n3. **Configurable stall timeout** per model via the catalog entry (some models legitimately think longer than others).\n4. **Emit a structured event in the session log** (currently the stall is only visible as an error string in sessions.jsonl). New event type `reasoning.stall` with model, timeout_ms, reasoning_tail, prompt_id.\n\n## Counterpart in benchmark harness\n\nThe lucebox-hub/dflash/scripts/bench_server.py harness will be extended to count stall rate as a benchmark metric — this requires the structured error.",

Error context includes the last N reasoning tokens (default 500, configurable).\n3. Per-model stall timeout configurable via the model catalog (modelcatalog/catalog.go).\n4. New session-log event `reasoning.stall` emitted with model, timeout_ms, reasoning_tail, prompt_id.\n5. Test fixture exercises the stall path against a stub provider that emits only reasoning tokens past the timeout, asserting structured error and event emission."

# AGENTS.md instructions for <HOME>/Projects/niflheim

<INSTRUCTIONS>
# AGENTS.md - Niflheim AI Coding Guidelines

## Quick Reference

```bash
# Bootstrap the required local toolchain and gate binaries
scripts/ensure-dev-tools.sh --scope hooks

# Build and test with the repo-pinned Rust toolchain
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo build --workspace
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo test --workspace --exclude niflheim-contract-tests
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo test -p niflheim-contract-tests    # Requires postgres + Docker + libgit2
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo test -p niflheim-integration-tests # Integration tests (cross-crate)
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo test -p niflheim-e2e               # End-to-end tests

# Quality gates (must pass before commit; aligned in lefthook.yml and .github/workflows/)
scripts/ci-local.sh                     # Local act wrapper: default lint+clippy
scripts/ci-local.sh full               # Full Phase0 workflow via act
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo fmt --all -- --check
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings -D clippy::todo -D clippy::unimplemented -D clippy::dbg_macro -D clippy::print_stdout -D clippy::unwrap_used
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo deny check
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo machete crates tools
scripts/check-transaction-semantics.sh
scripts/check-acceptance-policy.sh
scripts/check-acceptance-traceability.sh
scripts/check-acceptance-coverage.sh

# Canonical "run everything" gate
lefthook run pre-commit
```

## Project Structure

```
crates/                    # Core libraries (production code)
  niflheim-core/          # Types, errors, configuration
  niflheim-control/       # Control plane, leases, coordination
  niflheim-ingest/        # Event ingestion pipeline
  niflheim-protocol/      # Kafka, pgwire protocol handlers
  niflheim-query/         # SQL engine, DataFusion integration
  niflheim-storage/       # WAL, cold tier, S3

tools/                     # CLI tools and harnesses
  niflheim-cli/           # Main CLI application
  bench-harness/          # Benchmark infrastructure
  postgres-harness/       # Test postgres setup
  sql-submit/             # SQL submission helper tool
  test-data-generator/    # Synthetic data generation
  pgwire-server/          # PostgreSQL wire protocol server
  connectors/             # External connectors (Python, managed with uv)
    datagen/              # Synthetic data generator connector (SD-019)
    hubspot/              # HubSpot reference connector (SD-019)
    marketo/              # Marketo reference connector (SD-019)

tests/                     # Test suites
  contract/               # Contract tests - verify external APIs
  integration/            # Integration tests - cross-crate behavior
  e2e/                    # End-to-end tests - full system flows

spikes/                    # Experimental code (excluded from workspace)
docs/                      # Documentation and ADRs
```

## Rust Standards

**Edition**: 2024. **MSRV**: 1.94.0. Run `cargo fmt --all` after changes.

Workspace clippy lints (`Cargo.toml`): `all`, `pedantic`, `nursery` at warn; `todo`, `unimplemented`,
`dbg_macro`, `print_stdout`, `unwrap_used` at deny. The pre-commit hook runs clippy with `-D warnings`,
turning all warnings into errors.

**Lint inheritance**: Every crate in the workspace inherits workspace lints via `[lints] workspace = true`.
New crates must include this in their `Cargo.toml` and pass `cargo clippy -p <crate> --all-targets
--no-deps -- -D warnings` before merge.

Style: collapse nested ifs, inline format args (`format!("{x}")`), method refs over closures
(`.map(String::as_str)`), explicit match arms over wildcards.

**Unsafe policy**: `unsafe_code = "deny"` at the workspace level in `Cargo.toml`. Any `unsafe` block
requires a `// SAFETY:` comment and a local `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` attribute.

Use `thiserror` for library error types, `anyhow` for applications. Never `.unwrap()` in library code.
Public API must have `///` docs for new/changed exported items.

## Toolchain Bootstrap

- `rust-toolchain.toml` and `Cargo.toml` `workspace.package.rust-version` are authoritative and must stay in lockstep.
- Run `scripts/ensure-dev-tools.sh --scope hooks` on a new machine before build, test, or hook work.
- Repo-owned Rust commands must run through `scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh`; do not rely on ambient `cargo`, `rustc`, or `rustfmt` from an arbitrary shell PATH.
- Do not use `RUSTC_WRAPPER=` or similar overrides to bypass `.cargo/config.toml`. If `sccache` or the pinned toolchain is missing, bootstrap it or stop.
- Use `scripts/ci-local.sh` for pre-push local CI via `act`: the default runs `lint` then `clippy`, `scripts/ci-local.sh lint` and `scripts/ci-local.sh clippy` target those jobs directly, and `scripts/ci-local.sh full` runs the full `.github/workflows/phase0-architecture-gates.yml` pipeline.

## Testing, Coverage, and Acceptance

See [`docs/AGENTS-testing.md`](docs/AGENTS-testing.md) for the full testing guide including:
- Test levels, backends, and environment requirements
- Cross-path consistency rule (SQL INSERT / Kafka / COPY must all work)
- Acceptance-grade E2E test standards
- Source-line coverage with `cargo llvm-cov` and issue closeout rules
- Acceptance artifact conventions and `TP-*.acceptance.toml` rules

## Documentation Canon

- Start repo/docs orientation at `README.md`.
- V1 framing sources of truth are `docs/helix/01-frame/prd.md`, `docs/helix/01-frame/v1-capability-matrix.md`, `docs/helix/01-frame/terminology.md`, and `docs/helix/02-design/architecture.md`.
- If a lower-level contract or system-design doc conflicts with the V1 framing docs, do not propagate the legacy wording into new work. Translate to the canonical V1 model in new docs/tests and file or update an issue for the contract/design cleanup.

**Terminology rules for new user-facing docs, tests, and acceptance text:**
- In V1, `tenant` maps 1:1 to the top-level Postgres-compatible `database` boundary.
- Use `schema`, not `namespace`, unless you are explicitly discussing a legacy internal field that still needs cleanup.
- Use `table`, not `collection` or `dataset`, for user-visible behavior.
- Prefer `historical writes` or `time-agnostic ingestion` over `late arrivals`.

## AI Agent Rules

- Run focused checks first (`scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo test -p <crate> <test_name>`), then full quality gates before handoff.
- Bootstrap missing local tools; do not work around missing `sccache`, `rustup`, or the pinned Rust version with ad hoc env overrides.
- When proposing process, testing, constraint, or documentation best practices, first check the canonical `docs/AGENTS-*.md` file for that domain and extend it instead of inventing parallel guidance.
- List commands actually run in handoff notes; call out anything skipped.
- Do not claim performance changes without exact benchmark command and output.
- When implementing a feature that touches the write path, verify it works through ALL ingest paths (SQL INSERT, Kafka produce, COPY FROM STDIN) and survives ALL lifecycle operations (restart, compaction, retention delete, cold replay).
- When wiring a feature into the runtime (`niflheim-runtime/src/lib.rs`), verify the wiring is reachable by running `demo-test.sh` or an equivalent end-to-end test against the real binary.
- When reviewing specs, contracts, or acceptance coverage, treat unsupported behavior and scope exclusions as first-class requirements.
- Correctness-critical allocators and fences (offsets, epochs, request IDs, watermarks) must not silently fall back to sentinel values on contention or missing state.
- When changing docs/specs/contracts, keep the root `README.md`, the terminology doc, and the V1 capability matrix aligned with the behavior change.
- If `lefthook` or a similar gate fails solely because of unrelated pre-existing dirty files outside your change set, do not reformat or stage those files just to satisfy the hook.

## Dependencies

Managed via `cargo-deny` (`deny.toml`). `cargo deny check` covers licenses, registries, and advisories.

Adding a dependency: add to `[workspace.dependencies]` in root `Cargo.toml`, reference with
`{ workspace = true }` in crate `Cargo.toml`, run `cargo deny check`.

## Performance

See [`tools/bench-harness/AGENTS.md`](tools/bench-harness/AGENTS.md) for benchmark commands, profiling, ratchets, and optimization patterns.
See [`crates/niflheim-storage/AGENTS.md`](crates/niflheim-storage/AGENTS.md) for WAL format, hot/cold tier architecture, and write modes.
See [`crates/niflheim-protocol/AGENTS.md`](crates/niflheim-protocol/AGENTS.md) for Kafka-specific learnings.
See [SD-011: Pipeline Performance Model](docs/helix/02-design/system-design/SD-011-pipeline-performance-model.md) for the full performance framework.

## Current Delivery Scope (Local First, Cold Active)

- Local NVMe efficiency remains the primary optimization target and the first place regressions must be eliminated.
- Cold-tier durability, validation, file lifecycle management, and failure behavior are active production surfaces, not deferred future work.
- In scope now: local WAL/materialization correctness and performance, control-plane ownership and WAL/file-state alignment, async cold export/copy, SQL query via DataFusion + pgwire, CDC runtime/export, secondary indexes, MGCC row augmentation, durable-mode latency/throughput gating, cold-tier object fanout/cost discipline, and cold-tier failure chaos/perf gates.
- Not in concrete V1 design discussions unless explicitly promoted: alternative interface layers (for example MCP), KV lookup, real-time subscriptions, and multi-region.

## Transaction Semantics and System Constraints

See [`docs/AGENTS-constraints.md`](docs/AGENTS-constraints.md) for the full reference including:
- Transaction visibility model (autocommit vs explicit vs `niflheim_sync()`)
- Key invariants (buffered UPDATE/DELETE, read guards, ROLLBACK)
- Testing transaction code
- Complete system constraints table with ADR/SD sources
- Canonical reference: `docs/helix/02-design/contracts/SEM-001-transaction-durability-visibility.md`

## Worktree Workflow (`wt`)

Use `wt` (worktrunk) to manage parallel worktrees for feature branches.

```bash
wt list                          # List worktrees and their status
wt switch --create my-feature    # Create a new feature branch + worktree
wt switch my-feature             # Switch to an existing worktree
wt switch -                      # Switch back to previous worktree
wt switch ^                      # Switch to main
wt merge                         # Merge current branch into main
wt remove                        # Remove a worktree and delete its branch if merged
```

**AI agent workflow:** `wt switch --create <branch> -x claude -- 'Fix the null pointer in query.rs'`

## Issue Tracking with helix tracker

**IMPORTANT**: This project uses **ddx bead** for ALL issue tracking. Do NOT use markdown TODOs, task lists, or other tracking methods.

Canonical storage is managed by `ddx bead`; do not hard-code a storage pathname.

```bash
helix tracker ready --json                              # Check for ready work
helix tracker create "Title" --type task --deps parent  # Create new issue
helix tracker show <id> --json                          # Show details
helix tracker update <id> --claim                       # Claim work
helix tracker close <id>                                # Complete work
helix tracker dep add <child> <parent>                  # Add dependency
helix tracker status --json                             # Overview
```

**Workflow:** Check ready work -> claim -> implement -> commit -> close. Discover new work? Create linked issue with `--deps`. Do NOT create markdown TODO lists.

## Landing the Plane (Session Completion)

Work is NOT complete until `git push` succeeds.

1. **File issues** for remaining work
2. **Run quality gates** (if code changed)
3. **Update issue status** — close finished work, update in-progress items
4. **Push**: `git pull --rebase && git push && git status`
5. **Verify** all changes committed AND pushed
6. **Hand off** — provide context for next session

**CRITICAL:** NEVER stop before pushing. NEVER say "ready to push when you are" — YOU must push. If push fails, resolve and retry.

# Benchmark Harness

## Benchmark Commands

```bash
# Self-contained end-to-end (spins up embedded Niflheim server):
cargo run --release -p bench-harness --bin integrated_pipeline_bench -- --records 100000

# Against an external production server on NVMe:
cargo run --release -p bench-harness --bin integrated_pipeline_bench -- \
  --external --kafka-broker localhost:9092 \
  --pgwire-host localhost --pgwire-port 5433 \
  --records 1000000

# JSON output for CI regression tracking:
cargo run --release -p bench-harness --bin integrated_pipeline_bench -- \
  --records 100000 --output json

# Isolated delta-rs Parquet write benchmark (hx-12b3b247)
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo run --release -p bench-harness --bin delta_write_bench -- \
  --rows 1000000 --output .helix-logs/hx-12b3b247-delta-write-bench.json

# Dedup hot-path benchmark (B5 / hx-d127e54c)
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo run -p bench-harness --bin dedup_hot_path_bench -- \
  --rows 50000 --unique-keys 5000 --iterations 8 \
  --output .helix-logs/hx-d127e54c-dedup-hot-path.json

# Checkpoint A closure lane (16-producer throughput + 1-producer p95 latency)
scripts/benchmark-checkpoint-a.sh

# WAL baseline proof
cargo run -p postgres-harness --bin pgwire-insert-wal-proof -- \
  --target-mib 100 --payload-bytes 1024 --batch-rows 10000 --write-mode tracked
# Or: scripts/prove-wal-100mb.sh
```

Use debug builds for iteration; reserve `--release` for milestone measurements.
sccache is configured but changing niflheim-protocol invalidates ~4 dependent crates (~10 min release).

## Profiling

```bash
scripts/profile-pipeline.sh                          # Dev build, JSON/report artifacts under /tmp
scripts/profile-pipeline.sh --release --iterations 3 # Release helper with repeated runs
scripts/profile-pipeline.sh --no-build --release     # Reuse existing binary
scripts/profile-pipeline.sh --release --profile      # Compatibility flag; notes profiling gap in the report
```

Output: `/tmp/niflheim-profile-<timestamp>/` (JSON, markdown, per-run stderr logs, invocation metadata).

## Current Scope (Phase 1: Hot Tier Local Disks)

- Current delivery target is hot-tier correctness and performance on local disks.
- Benchmark gating in this phase is based on hot-tier behavior (`fire_and_forget`, `tracked`) and protocol hot-path throughput/latency.
- Cold-tier durability/performance (`durable`, S3/MinIO timing, PUT cost/latency) is explicitly Phase 2 work.
- For every benchmark report, state whether the run is `hot-tier-only` or `cold-tier`.

## Benchmark Rules

- Canonical performance claims use `integrated_pipeline_bench` with 4 stages: Kafka produce, materialization, COUNT verification, and full scan.
- Throughput math: use actual wire bytes for protocol stages, not logical payload assumptions.
- If using `--external`, verify the server is on the expected hardware (NVMe, etc.) before citing numbers.
- Commit harnesses/scripts; keep generated artifacts out of git.

## Baselines, Hot Path Maps, and Optimization Targets

See [SD-011: Pipeline Performance Model](../../docs/helix/02-design/system-design/SD-011-pipeline-performance-model.md) for current baselines (§7), hot path maps (§8), and optimization targets (§9).

## Physics-Based Efficiency Ratchets

The ratchet system prevents performance regressions by comparing Niflheim's throughput against
raw hardware capabilities (sequential write, fsync, Parquet read/write, memcpy). Efficiency
ratios express what fraction of hardware ceiling our code achieves. Ratchet floors ensure
these ratios never decrease.

**Key files:**
- `scripts/fio-io-baseline.sh` — measures raw disk I/O ceiling with fio (cached by hardware identity)
- `scripts/fixtures/io-baseline-{hash}.json` — content-addressed fio results per machine
- `scripts/fixtures/perf-ratchets.json` — efficiency ratio floors and last-measured values
- `scripts/perf-regression-check.sh` — gate script that runs benchmarks and checks both throughput and ratchets

**Running the system:**

```bash
# Measure raw disk I/O ceiling with fio (auto-cached by hardware identity)
scripts/fio-io-baseline.sh

# Re-verify reopened SD-011 checkpoints on their dedicated canonical lanes
scripts/benchmark-checkpoint-a.sh
scripts/benchmark-checkpoint-b.sh
scripts/benchmark-checkpoint-c.sh
scripts/benchmark-checkpoint-d.sh

# Sweep alternate Delta writer tuning on any checkpoint wrapper
BENCHMARK_CHECKPOINT_PARQUET_ROW_GROUP_SIZE=1000000 \
BENCHMARK_CHECKPOINT_ZSTD_LEVEL=0 \
scripts/benchmark-checkpoint-c.sh

# Full regression gate: runs benchmark, compares throughput + efficiency ratchets
scripts/perf-regression-check.sh

# Update throughput baseline after intentional performance changes
scripts/perf-regression-check.sh --update-baseline

# Tighten ratchet floors to current efficiency ratios (ratchets only go up)
scripts/perf-regression-check.sh --update-ratchets

# Force ratchet floors down (after known hardware change or intentional trade-off)
scripts/perf-regression-check.sh --update-ratchets --force
```

**How efficiency ratios work (v2, per ADR-043):**
- `produce_io_efficiency` = E2E Kafka produce MB/s / fio seq_write @ 128K
- `materialize_io_efficiency` = Delta materialize MB/s / fio seq_write @ 128K
- `scan_io_efficiency` = Query full-scan MB/s / fio seq_read @ 128K
- `combined_io_efficiency` = WAL + materialize concurrent MB/s / fio seq_write @ 128K

During transition, the gate also accepts v1 `efficiency` ratios from the benchmark until
the benchmark is updated to emit `io_efficiency` (see niflheim-589c).

For reopened SD-011 checkpoint issues, prefer the dedicated checkpoint refresh scripts over the
full gate when the scorecard calls for a canonical isolated lane.

Each ratio has a `floor` (minimum acceptable) and `measured` (last observed). The gate fails if
any measured ratio drops below `floor * (1 - tolerance_pct/100)`. When `--update-ratchets` is
used, floors are tightened to `measured * (1 - tolerance_pct/100)` but never lowered without
`--force`.

Ratchet checks and `--update-ratchets` run three benchmark samples by default
(`PERF_RATCHET_SAMPLE_COUNT=3`). The final report uses the median
`materialize_io_efficiency` and `scan_io_efficiency` values because same-host
single samples have shown threshold-crossing variance for these non-WAL ratios.
Set `PERF_RATCHET_SAMPLE_COUNT=1` only for local diagnostic runs.

## PGO (Profile-Guided Optimization)

PGO improves materialize +12% and scan +10% by optimizing branch layout and
inlining based on actual execution profiles. Requires `cargo-pgo`:

```bash
# Install cargo-pgo (one-time)
cargo install cargo-pgo --locked

# Step 1: Instrumented build
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo pgo build -- -p bench-harness --bin integrated_pipeline_bench

# Step 2: Training run (generates profile data)
LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=target/pgo-profiles/bench_%m_%p.profraw \
  RUST_LOG=error target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/integrated_pipeline_bench --records 100000

# Step 3: Optimized build
scripts/with-pinned-rust.sh cargo pgo optimize build -- -p bench-harness --bin integrated_pipeline_bench

# Step 4: Run optimized binary
target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/integrated_pipeline_bench --records 1000000 --output json
```

## Key Optimization Patterns

- WAL encoding must be protocol-neutral via `niflheim-wal-codec` -- do not duplicate per protocol.
- Use zero-copy serialization (`WalValueRef<'a>`) instead of cloning owned values on hot paths.
- Use `Bytes::clone()` (Arc increment) instead of `Bytes::copy_from_slice()`.
- Debug builds for iteration; release only for milestone measurements.
- WAL concurrency: per-connection tasks run in parallel; hot writer mutex holds only for memcpy (~100-200us).
- Never block the flush thread for I/O that isn't on the critical path (e.g. fsync of completed segments).
  Background threads are fine for short-lived, self-terminating operations like segment fsync.

# AGENTS.md instructions for <HOME>/Projects/ddx

<INSTRUCTIONS>
# DDx Agent Instructions

This repository uses DDx's built-in bead tracker for durable work management.

## Default Interactive Mode

When an agent is opened in this repository without an explicit execution
directive, the default mode is **`queue_steward`**: survey, triage, and
advise on the DDx bead queue without claiming or editing anything unless
the user explicitly asks.

| Mode | Trigger | Allowed | Prohibited |
|---|---|---|---|
| `queue_steward` | Broad DDx questions: "what's on the queue", "what's ready", "how am I doing", "do work" without an explicit worker directive | Read tracker and docs; report status; advise on bead quality; run `ddx bead list/ready/status/show` | Claiming or editing beads; starting `ddx work`/`ddx try` autonomously |
| `bead_execution` | Explicit worker directive: `ddx work`, `ddx try <id>`, `ddx agent execute-bead`, or `execute-bead` harness invocation | Full execute-bead lifecycle per the bead body | Scope creep outside the named bead |
| `direct_user_implementation` | User explicitly asks to edit code or docs ("fix this bug", "update this file") | Edit code and docs as instructed; commit to the current branch | Draining the bead queue autonomously |
| `review` | User explicitly asks for a review ("review this PR", "grade this bead") | Read-only evidence-based review per §Reviewer Mode | Writing commits or claiming beads |

**`bead_execution` supersedes `queue_steward`** when DDx invokes a worker
explicitly. Tracker, merge-policy, and safety instructions remain
load-bearing across all modes.

Execution-ready beads belong to `ddx work` (or an explicit `ddx try <id>`).
Do not start execution unless the user explicitly requests direct implementation.

## Bead Policy

- Treat `.ddx/beads.jsonl` as DDx-managed data, not as a hand-edited document.
- Create beads only with `ddx bead create`. Before filing, conform to `docs/helix/06-iterate/bead-authoring-template.md` — descriptions + AC must be standalone (no `/tmp/*`, no chat refs), cite root cause by file:line, name specific `Test*` symbols, and include the `cd cli && go test ./<pkg>/...` + `lefthook run pre-commit` gate. Sub-agent execution depends on this floor (principle P7).
- See docs/helix/06-iterate/reliability-principles.md for the 7 reliability principles applied to ddx try / ddx work execution.
- Modify bead metadata only with `ddx bead update`.
- Manage dependencies only with `ddx bead dep add` and `ddx bead dep remove`.
- Close work only with `ddx bead close`.
- Use `ddx bead import` and `ddx bead export` for bulk migration or interchange.
- Commit tracker mutations by default after bead commands.
- If the tracker change stands alone, make a tracker-only commit promptly.
- If it belongs to related implementation/docs work already being prepared for
  commit, fold the tracker change into that same commit instead of leaving
  `.ddx/beads.jsonl` dirty.

## When filing beads — bead-authoring template

Every bead must satisfy the 8-criterion rubric documented in
`docs/helix/06-iterate/bead-authoring-template.md` before it is filed
or dispatched to a sub-agent. The bead body is the entire prompt the
sub-agent will see; if a competent agent given only the bead text
cannot pick a file to edit and run tests without asking, the bead
must be retrofitted before dispatch.

Required template fields: title (imperative + subsystem), description
with PROBLEM + ROOT CAUSE WITH FILE:LINE + PROPOSED FIX + NON-SCOPE,
numbered AC including specific `Test*` names + `cd cli && go test ...`
+ `lefthook run pre-commit`, labels (phase + area + kind + cross-refs),
and explicit parent + deps.

Do not cite `/tmp/...` plan files as load-bearing context — they do
not survive between machines or sessions. Inline the relevant excerpt
into the description instead.

## Merge Policy

Branches containing execute-bead or execute-loop commits carry a
per-attempt execution audit trail in their git history. This trail is
load-bearing data, not noise:

- `chore: update tracker (execute-bead <TIMESTAMP>)` — one commit per
  attempt; the timestamp is the attempt ID.
- `Merge bead <bead-id> attempt <TIMESTAMP>- into <branch>` — the merge
  commit that lands a successful attempt from its isolated worktree.
- `feat|fix|refactor|...: ... [ddx-<id>]` — the substantive bead work,
  tagged with the bead ID.

Bead records store `closing_commit_sha` as a pointer back into git
history; cost, latency, retry, and tier-escalation reports read these
commits directly. Any SHA rewrite breaks the pointers and destroys the
`output = bead(input)` accuracy the system is built on.

**NO HISTORY REWRITING on execute-bead branches.** The only acceptable
merge strategies are:

1. **Plain fast-forward** — when the target is a strict ancestor of the
   feature branch: `git merge --ff-only` + `git push`. No new commits.
2. **Merge commit** — when divergence exists: `git merge --no-ff`.
   Creates a 2-parent merge; the feature branch commits remain intact.

Never use on an execute-bead branch:

- `gh pr merge --squash` — collapses every attempt into one commit.
- `gh pr merge --rebase` — GitHub's rebase-merge replays commits as NEW
  SHAs, breaking `closing_commit_sha` pointers.
- `git rebase -i` with `fixup`, `squash`, `drop`, or `reword` — rewrites
  SHAs.
- `git filter-branch` / `git filter-repo` stripping "chore" commits — same.
- `git commit --amend` on any commit already in the trail — same.

When in doubt, check `git log <branch> --oneline | grep -E 'execute-bead|\[ddx-'`.
If any match, preserve history on the merge.

The `pre-push` hook in `lefthook.yml` (`merge-policy` command) enforces
this: if a push would drop execute-bead or `[ddx-*]` commits the remote
already has — i.e. a force-push rewriting that history — the hook
rejects it. Do not disable this hook to work around it; the right move
is to keep the commits intact and use `--ff-only` or a `--no-ff` merge.

## Prohibited Actions

- Do not edit `.ddx/beads.jsonl` manually.
- Do not add, remove, or rewrite bead rows with `apply_patch`, editors, scripts, or ad hoc JSONL manipulation.
- Do not invent bead IDs or prefixes such as `hx-*` or `ddx-*`.
- Do not treat nearby tracker entries as a naming pattern to copy.
- Do not squash, rebase, or filter branches containing execute-bead commits (see Merge Policy above).

## If The CLI Seems Insufficient

- Prefer the nearest supported `ddx bead` command.
- If the required tracker operation is not supported by `ddx bead`, stop and ask rather than editing tracker storage directly.

## Verification

- Use `ddx bead show <id>` to inspect one bead.
- Use `ddx bead list`, `ddx bead ready`, and `ddx bead status` to inspect queue state.
- Use `ddx bead --help` and `ddx bead create --help` before assuming a flag exists.

## Skill Policy

- Treat `SKILL.md` frontmatter as a strict interface, not freeform metadata.
- Published DDx skills must use top-level YAML frontmatter fields `name` and `description`.
- Use `argument-hint` only when the skill accepts a trailing positional or shorthand invocation hint.
- Do not use nested `skill:` frontmatter for DDx repo skills.
- Run `ddx skills check [path ...]` for reusable validation across repo skills and plugin skills.
- Run `make skill-schema` after editing any file under `skills/*/SKILL.md` or `cli/internal/skills/*/SKILL.md`.

## Reviewer Mode

- When a task explicitly calls for no-tool reviewer mode, keep the pass
  read-only and evidence-based. That convention is the structured-evidence
  review mode described in TD-033; do not attach tools mid-pass.
- Prefer the supplied artifacts and repo files over exploratory tool use.
- If you need a factual citation, point to the smallest relevant file:line
  span and avoid broad re-reading of unrelated context.

# DDx

DDx (Document-Driven Development eXperience) is a CLI platform for
document-driven development. It ships a bead tracker (portable work
items with acceptance criteria), a task-execution boundary (DDx
forwards raw passthrough constraints for harness, provider, model,
model-ref, and profile while power travels as `MinPower`/`MaxPower`
bounds; Fizeau owns concrete routing, provider/model discovery,
aliases, fuzzy matching, catalog lookups, and transcript/session
rendering), a persona system (bindable AI personalities), a library
registry (plugins with prompts, templates, personas), and git-aware
synchronization. This skill makes any skills-compatible coding agent
(Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, etc.) understand and operate
the DDx surface correctly.

## How this skill works

The skill body you're reading is an **overview** plus an **intent
router**. The real domain guidance lives in `reference/*.md` files.

**Directive: before responding to any DDx-related request, read the
matching reference file from the router table below. The router is
not optional — your answer must be grounded in the reference file's
guidance, not this overview alone.**

## Vocabulary

Single source of truth for DDx terms. Every reference file uses these
exact definitions.

- **Bead** — a portable work item (task, bug, epic, chore) with
  metadata, dependencies, and acceptance criteria. `ddx bead create`.
- **Queue** — the set of active beads. The *execution-ready queue* is
  `status=open` work whose dependencies are closed and which is not parked by
  cooldown, supersession, or execution-eligibility policy. `ddx bead ready`,
  `ddx bead status`.
- **Lifecycle status** — the persisted bead state: `proposed`, `open`,
  `in_progress`, `blocked`, `closed`, or `cancelled`.
- **Ready** — a bead whose dependencies are all closed and which is
  eligible to be picked up next. `ddx bead ready`.
- **Blocked** — `status=blocked` work paused by a hard external recheckable
  blocker. Ordinary dependency waits are derived queue state, not blocked
  status. `ddx bead blocked`.
- **Proposed** — work awaiting operator decision before autonomous execution.
  Proposed beads are not worker-eligible until accepted, rewritten, split,
  blocked externally, cancelled, or otherwise resolved.
- **Claim** — mark a bead as in-progress by an agent (concurrent-write
  protection). `ddx bead update <id> --claim`.
- **Close** — mark a bead as done, with evidence (session, commit
  SHA). `ddx bead close <id>`. Beads only close on execution outcomes
  `success` or `already_satisfied`.
- **Run** — one task invocation atom. `ddx run` calls Fizeau `Execute`
  once with prompt/config, `MinPower`/`MaxPower` bounds, and optional
  raw passthrough constraints.
- **Try** — one bead attempt in an isolated worktree. `ddx try <id>` wraps
  `ddx run` with bead prompt resolution, evidence capture, and merge/preserve
  finalization.
- **Work** — drain the bead queue. `ddx work` picks ready beads and invokes
  `ddx try`; it owns queue iteration and retry policy.
- **Execution** — a generic DDx execution run (FEAT-010). Includes execution
  definitions, execution records, and execution evidence under `.ddx/runs/<id>/`.
- **Agent** — an AI coding agent (Claude, Codex, Gemini, etc.)
  invoked via a harness. Not a subagent (harness-specific — see
  below).
- **Harness** — a Fizeau routing concept. DDx may pass `--harness` as
  an operator-supplied constraint, but DDx does not validate, rank, fallback, or
  branch on harness names.
- **Persona** — a Markdown file (YAML frontmatter + body) that
  defines an AI personality. DDx injects the body as a system-prompt
  addendum to `ddx run`. `ddx persona list/show/bind`.
- **Role** — an abstract function (e.g., `code-reviewer`,
  `test-engineer`) a workflow can reference. Projects bind roles to
  personas.
- **Binding** — a project-specific `role: persona` map in
  `.ddx/config.yaml` under `persona_bindings`.
- **Power bounds** — `MinPower` and optional `MaxPower` integers passed to the
  upstream execution service. DDx may raise `MinPower` on eligible retries;
  Fizeau owns concrete route selection within those bounds.
- **Plugin** — a self-contained extension installed to
  `.ddx/plugins/<name>/`. The default `ddx` plugin (personas,
  prompts, patterns, templates) is auto-installed by `ddx init`.
  `ddx install <name>`.
- **Skill** — an agentskills.io-standard directory (SKILL.md +
  optional `reference/`, `evals/`, `scripts/`). This `ddx` skill is
  the one DDx ships. Plugins can ship additional skills.
- **Subagent** — a harness-local concept for running a prompt in an
  isolated context (Claude Code's `.claude/agents/` + `context:
  fork`; Codex's `agents/`; others differ). DDx does not specify subagent
  orchestration; that remains harness business.
- **Update** — refresh plugin/toolkit content to a newer version.
  `ddx update [<plugin>]`.
- **Upgrade** — replace the DDx binary with a newer release.
  `ddx upgrade`.
- **Review** — two distinct concepts. **Bead review**
  (`ddx bead review <id>`) grades a completed bead against its
  acceptance criteria. **Comparison/adversarial review** is a workflow skill
  composition over `ddx run`, not a core quorum flag. See `reference/review.md`.
- **Governing artifact** — the document that authorizes a bead's
  work: a FEAT-\*, SD-\*, TD-\*, or ADR-\* under `docs/`. Referenced
  via `spec-id`.
- **Spec-id** — the `spec-id: <ID>` custom field on a bead pointing
  at its governing artifact.

## Top-level policy reminders

These apply across all DDx operations. Do not restate them in every
reference file; do not violate them.

- **Never edit `.ddx/beads.jsonl` directly.** All tracker changes go
  through `ddx bead create/update/close/dep`. Direct edits corrupt
  bead history and cannot be audited.
- **Tracker changes are commit-worthy.** After `ddx bead create`,
  `update`, `dep add/remove`, or `close`, commit the resulting
  `.ddx/beads.jsonl` change — either as a tracker-only commit or
  folded into the same commit as related implementation changes.
- **Preserve bead-attempt commit history.** Branches containing
  `ddx try` / `ddx work` execution commits carry an audit trail. **Never
  squash, rebase, filter, or amend** these commits. Use only
  `git merge --ff-only` or `git merge --no-ff` when merging.
  `gh pr merge --squash` and `--rebase` are forbidden on these
  branches.
- **Work in worktrees for parallel agents.** Use `wt switch -c
  <branch>` (worktrunk) or equivalent to give each concurrent agent
  its own isolated checkout. `ddx try` does this automatically;
  manual parallel work should too.
- **Power-first execution dispatch.** Default to `ddx run`/`ddx try`/`ddx work`
  with power bounds. `--harness`, `--provider`, and `--model` are passthrough
  constraints only; DDx must not use them for routing policy.

# Review — Bead Review and Quorum Review

## Mode note

This reference covers **explicit `review` mode**: requests that name review as
the primary action — "review this", "check against spec", `ddx bead review <id>`.

If the user said "review with fresh eyes", "fold in this guidance and review
again", or any broad orientation phrase, they are in **`interactive-steward`**
mode — see `reference/interactive.md` for the fresh-eyes review and fold-guidance
phases. Multi-harness adversarial review is consent-gated in steward mode.

Review mode is **read-only** by default. Code edits only happen if the user
explicitly requests fixes after seeing the findings.

---

DDx has two distinct review concepts. They are **not interchangeable**.

| Concept | Command | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Bead review** | `ddx bead review <id>` | Grades a bead's implementation against its declared acceptance criteria. Per-AC verdict with evidence. |
| **Comparison/adversarial review** | workflow skill composition over `ddx run` | Dispatches review prompts across multiple roles or configured agent routes and aggregates the verdicts. Used for high-stakes or adversarial checks. |

## Bead review

```bash
ddx bead review <bead-id>
```

Generates a review-ready prompt that includes:

- Bead title, description, acceptance criteria (verbatim).
- Governing artifact content (follows `spec-id`).
- The diff since the bead's base commit (execution evidence commits
  excluded — see the related bug ddx-39e27896 for exclusion
  pathspec).
- Review instructions: output contract, verdict taxonomy.

The reviewer (whoever receives the prompt — a human, `ddx run`, or a workflow
skill composition) produces a structured verdict:

```
## Bead review: ddx-<id>

### Verdict: APPROVE | REQUEST_CHANGES | BLOCK

### Per-criterion

1. [AC text]
   Verdict: APPROVE | REQUEST_CHANGES | BLOCK
   Evidence: <file:line, test output, diff hunk, or explicit "not verifiable">

2. [AC text]
   ...

### Summary
<1-3 sentences of overall context>

### Findings
<detailed issues, if any; omit when verdict is APPROVE with no findings>
```

The review output can be stored as bead evidence:

```bash
ddx bead evidence add <id> --type review --body <path-to-review.md>
```

## Comparison/adversarial review

```bash
ddx run --persona code-reviewer --prompt review-prompt.md > review-code.md
ddx run --persona architect --prompt review-prompt.md > review-arch.md
```

Aggregation policies used by workflow skills:

- `majority` — at least ⌈N/2⌉ harnesses must agree on the verdict.
- `unanimous` — all harnesses must agree.
- `any` — pass if any harness APPROVES (rarely useful; adversarial
  checks should require stronger consensus).

Use comparison/adversarial review when:

- The change is high-stakes (migrations, security surface, API
  contracts, auth).
- The review surface is controversial and one harness's opinion
  isn't enough.
- You want adversarial pressure against a single-model blindspot
  (different model families have different failure modes).

The aggregated output shows each harness's verdict side-by-side plus
the aggregate decision. Disagreements are surfaced, not hidden.

## Required evidence format

Both review kinds share an evidence contract: **no verdict without
evidence.**

- "APPROVE" with no `Evidence:` lines → reject as malformed.
- "REQUEST_CHANGES" without pointing at the change needed → reject.
- "BLOCK" without a reason → reject (see the related bug
  ddx-39e27896 about `review-malfunction` retries).

Evidence takes one of these forms:

1. **File:line reference**: `cli/internal/bead/store.go:142`
2. **Test output**: `FAIL: TestBeadClose_UnclaimsOnNonSuccess (0.01s)`
3. **Diff hunk**: a short quote from the diff showing the offending
   or approved change.
4. **Explicit "not verifiable"**: the AC is written in a way that
   cannot be mechanically checked; flag this as a bead-authoring
   issue rather than silently approving.

## Anti-patterns

- **Hallucinated approval.** "Looks good to me!" with no per-AC
  grading. The review is worthless.
- **Reviewing the prompt instead of the diff.** The reviewer evaluated
  "what you intended" not "what you actually changed." Verdict must
  reference the diff or the resulting code.
- **Verdict without evidence.** Every verdict must have at least one
  evidence line; APPROVE is no exception (evidence can be "AC met:
  `go test ./foo/... passes` output attached").
- **Silencing disagreement in comparison review.** If two reviewers disagree,
  don't collapse to a single "decision." Surface the disagreement
  in the output and let the human decide.
- **Comparison review for routine work.** Single-reviewer bead review is fine
  for most beads. Reserve multi-reviewer comparison for the cases that justify the
  cost.

## Subagents: not this skill's business

Some harnesses can run a comparison in forked/isolated subagent
contexts; each harness implements this differently. This skill
doesn't specify how isolation is achieved —
`ddx run` is the portable invocation, and the harness decides whether to fork,
spawn, or run inline.

## CLI reference

```bash
# Bead review (single-reviewer AC grading)
ddx bead review <id>                           # generate review prompt
ddx bead review <id> --execute --harness claude  # dispatch and grade
ddx bead evidence add <id> --type review --body r.md  # store review

# Comparison review (workflow composition)
ddx run --persona code-reviewer --prompt review.md > review-code.md
ddx run --persona architect --prompt review.md > review-arch.md
```

Full flag list: `ddx bead review --help`, `ddx run --help`.

`*bead.WatcherHub` (`cli/internal/bead/watcher.go:36-66`) constructs its own `*Store` internally via `NewStore(projectID + "/.ddx")`. This bypasses any factory-level capability validation or backend selection. Today everything is JSONL so this is invisible; once AxonStore ships and `bead.backend: axon` is configured for production, the WatcherHub still polls a local JSONL file while the authoritative bead state lives in Lakebase Postgres. Result: silent stale-data bug — `beadLifecycle` GraphQL subscriptions return empty or stale events.

# ROOT CAUSE (file:line)
- `cli/internal/bead/watcher.go:54-66` — `SubscribeLifecycle` instantiates a `*Store` directly: `store := NewStore(projectID + "/.ddx")`. No injection point for the configured backend.
- `cli/internal/bead/watcher.go:60-65` — `newProjectWatcher(store, h.interval)` ties the watcher to that locally-constructed Store.
- `cli/internal/server/server.go` — constructs `*WatcherHub` and passes it to subscription resolvers. The hub is constructed once at server startup; the project Stores it creates internally are detached from any per-project factory.

# PROPOSED FIX
Change `WatcherHub` to take a `bead.BeadReader` (or `Backend`) factory function at construction:

```go
type StoreFactory func(projectID string) (bead.BeadReader, error)

type WatcherHub struct {
    factory  StoreFactory
    watchers map[string]*projectWatcher
    interval time.Duration
    ...
}

func NewWatcherHub(factory StoreFactory, interval time.Duration) *WatcherHub { ... }

func (h *WatcherHub) SubscribeLifecycle(ctx context.Context, projectID string) (<-chan LifecycleEvent, func(), error) {
    // ...
    store, err := h.factory(projectID)
    if err != nil { return nil, nil, err }
    pw = newProjectWatcher(store, h.interval)
    // ...
}
```

`cli/internal/server/server.go` is updated to pass a factory that uses the project's configured backend (selected via the same config pathway that the rest of ddx-server uses).

# NON-SCOPE
- Native subscription transport on AxonStore (separate work — would replace the polling-based `projectWatcher` with native push when available).
- Changing `LifecycleEvent` shape or semantics.
- Multi-tenant identity propagation (handled separately via the `bead.WithIdentity` ctx accessor pattern).
- Modifying callers other than `cli/internal/server/server.go` and the subscription resolver.

2. `cli/internal/bead/watcher.go` no longer contains a direct `NewStore(...)` call.

The bead interface refactor (`docs/helix/02-design/plan-2026-05-11-bead-backend-interfaces.md`) opens 5 categories of inadvertent regression that compile-time and test-time checks alone cannot catch:

1. **Direct file I/O against `.ddx/beads.jsonl`** outside the documented allowlist — encodes the file format into another package; silently breaks on schema changes.
2. **New types implementing `RawBackend`** for new backends — recreates the catastrophic whole-corpus-per-mutation problem that AxonBackend hit (see audit in `docs/plans/plan-2026-05-10-axon-only-architecture.md`).
3. **Untyped `ctx.Value(...)` calls in `cli/internal/bead/`** — `Context` becomes a god object, undermining the typed-accessor discipline.
4. **New callers holding `*bead.Store` as a struct field** when a narrower sub-interface would suffice — interface segregation (ISP) benefits never realized; future migration toward non-`*Store` impls (AxonStore) is harder.
5. **New `bead.NewStore(...)` calls** in production code outside the configured factory — bypasses capability validation and backend selection (Mock/prod divergence risk).

These categories are enumerated as side-doors S2, S3, S9, S1, S5+S6 in `docs/plans/plan-2026-05-11-bead-interface-integration.md`. The plan specifies enforcement via lint rules. This bead implements those lints.

# ROOT CAUSE
No lint coverage today. The integration plan calls for:

- `cli/tools/lints/direct-bead-jsonl-io` — flag `os.ReadFile/WriteFile/OpenFile/Create` against `beads.jsonl` or `beads-archive.jsonl` paths outside an allowlist.
- `cli/tools/lints/no-new-rawbackend-impls` — flag new types implementing `bead.RawBackend` outside the allowlist (`JSONLBackend`, `ExternalBackend`).
- `cli/tools/lints/typed-context-accessors-only` — flag `ctx.Value(...)` calls in `cli/internal/bead/` that don't go through a typed accessor.
- `cli/tools/lints/concrete-store-methods` — warn on new files in `cli/{cmd,internal/agent,internal/server,internal/escalation}` that introduce a `*bead.Store` field type when a narrower sub-interface would suffice.
- `cli/tools/lints/no-internal-store-construction` — flag `bead.NewStore(...)` calls outside test packages and the configured factory.

None of these exist today.

# PROPOSED FIX
Implement five Go analyzers (`golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis`) under `cli/tools/lints/`:

```
cli/tools/lints/
  Makefile                              # build the bead-lints binary
  cmd/bead-lints/main.go                # composes the 5 analyzers into a single vettool
  internal/
    directio/         analyzer.go       # direct-bead-jsonl-io
    rawbackend/       analyzer.go       # no-new-rawbackend-impls
    ctxaccessors/     analyzer.go       # typed-context-accessors-only
    concretestore/    analyzer.go       # concrete-store-methods
    nointernalstore/  analyzer.go       # no-internal-store-construction
  allowlist.yaml                        # maintained allowlist (paths + types + rationale)
```

Each analyzer:

- Reads `cli/tools/lints/allowlist.yaml` to know which files / types / packages are grandfathered.
- Reports violations as `analysis.Diagnostic` with `path:line: <message>`.

# AGENTS.md instructions for <HOME>/Projects/7thsense.scala-to-ts

<INSTRUCTIONS>
# Agent Instructions

## Issue Tracking

This project uses **bd** (beads) for issue tracking.
Run `bd prime` for workflow context, or install hooks with `bd hooks install`.

Quick reference:
- `bd ready` finds unblocked work
- `bd create "Title" --type task --priority 2` creates work
- `bd show <id>` shows the current acceptance criteria, dependencies, and close reason
- `bd close <id>` closes work
- `bd dolt push` pushes beads commits to a remote

## Learnings

- This clone uses a standalone local `.beads` database. Start or inspect its Dolt server from this checkout with `bd dolt start`, `bd dolt stop`, and `bd dolt status`.
- Beads state is synchronized explicitly through the local Dolt remote `file://<HOME>/Projects/7thsense-beads-remote`; use `bd dolt push` and `bd dolt pull` instead of a redirected shared `.beads` directory.
- For Scala coverage work, prefer the reusable coverage report helper instead of one-off XML parsing:
  - `python3 scripts/report_scoverage.py modules/lists/target/scala-2.13/coverage-report/cobertura.xml <class-or-file-filter>`
- `scripts/report_scoverage.py` distinguishes fully missed lines from partially covered lines; use that split before assuming a branch was never exercised.
- `com.networknt:json-schema-validator` 3.0.0 does not resolve `file:` schemas by default. For local shared-fixture validation, load the root schema from disk and map stable schema `$id` prefixes back to local `fixtures/` paths so sibling relative `$ref`s resolve without network fetches.
- `StringOrBooleanOrLong` tries `Boolean`, then `Long`, then `String` when decoding JSON. Numeric-looking JSON strings can therefore land in the `Long` branch; test helper behavior (`toLong`, `toString`) instead of asserting on the raw `Any` payload type.
- In the TypeScript contract harness, pre-register every schema under `fixtures/schemas/**` with Ajv using its `$id`. That is enough for stable `$id` plus relative `$ref` resolution without custom fetch hooks, and lets package tests prefer `fixtures/<component>` while still falling back to transitional local fixture directories.
- Scheduler helper coverage needs its own Vitest config because the package default only includes `src/**/*.ts`. Use `pnpm -C packages/scheduler test:contracts:coverage` to measure `tests/contracts/**/*.ts` together with `tests/parity/fixture-runner.test.ts`.
- `zio.logging.LogAnnotation` coverage is easiest to hit directly through `annotation.render.apply(value)`; creating a `LogContext` alone does not guarantee the render function executed.
- `zio.test.assertTrue` can fight implicit conversions on value classes like `JobId`; bind the converted primitive to a typed local before asserting if the macro starts inferring the wrapper type.
- After splitting pure contexts from runtime concerns, import `ss.utils.models.TContextRuntime.TContextRuntimeOps` anywhere runtime code still needs `.asLayer`, `.asLogContext`, or `.toLogContextValue`.
- Repo root discovery should use stable project markers like `build.sbt` and `project/`, not a hard-coded checkout directory name.
- Close each bead only after checks/tests pass, then make a dedicated git commit for that bead and stage only the files touched for that iteration.
- When moving GraphQL transport concerns out of `core/models`, put DTOs and scalar adapters under `interfaces/caliban` and add `Dependencies.ZIOCaliban` explicitly to any module that still imports Caliban types instead of relying on a transitive dependency from `models`.
- For Caliban schema assertions, prefer the reusable `CalibanSchemaSupport.renderSchema(...)` helper plus direct `Schema.resolve(...)` checks for custom scalars; that covers both rendered schema shape and scalar serialization without reintroducing annotations into domain models.
- When splitting an oversized `core/api` trait, keep the existing aggregate trait as a compatibility facade, move the focused method groups into new subtraits with any shared default helpers, and add a small mock-driven contract spec that exercises the new narrowed interfaces directly.
- Guice will not infer bindings for those new narrowed traits from an existing aggregate binding. Add explicit bindings for each new trait-to-implementation mapping in the composition root, even if they all point at the same concrete persistence class.
- On this workstation, Testcontainers can fail to keep Ryuk alive for postgres integration specs. If `infrastructure-postgres-it` dies with `testcontainers/ryuk` container startup errors, rerun with `TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true`.
- For the scheduler package, use `pnpm -C packages/scheduler test:portable:coverage` to measure the portable TypeScript surface (`tests/unit`, `tests/contracts`, `tests/parity`) without pulling in adapter or integration suites that need external services.
- Keep newly ported shared Stage 1 TypeScript shapes in `packages/scheduler/src/domain`, then re-export them through the existing scheduler model barrels so contract/parity code can adopt the shared types without a broad import-path rewrite.
- Portability acceptance criteria are split across beads and docs: check the child bead, its parent stage bead, `docs/plans/SCALA_TO_TS_PORT.md`, and the relevant `docs/portability/*inventory.md` entry before declaring boundary work complete.
- For Stage 3 boundary work, "retire" or "split" is stricter than "deprecated" or "added a narrower alias": verify callers actually migrate, confirm the oversized trait no longer carries the mixed responsibility, or create an explicit follow-up bead before closing the task.
- When extracting a narrowed `core/api` trait and adding Guice bindings, add at least one focused spec or compile-path check that exercises the new trait directly; wiring-only refactors are easy to close without proving the new seam is actually testable.


## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and file path so you can open the source for full instructions when using a specific skill.
### Available skills
- skill-creator: Guide for creating effective skills. This skill should be used when users want to create a new skill (or update an existing skill) that extends Codex's capabilities with specialized knowledge, workflows, or tool integrations. (file: <HOME>/.codex/skills/.system/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: <HOME>/.codex/skills/.system/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- slides: Build, edit, render, import, and export presentation decks with the preloaded @oai/artifact-tool JavaScript surface through the artifacts tool. (file: <HOME>/.codex/skills/.system/slides/SKILL.md)
- spreadsheets: Build, edit, recalculate, import, and export spreadsheet workbooks with the preloaded @oai/artifact-tool JavaScript surface through the artifacts tool. (file: <HOME>/.codex/skills/.system/spreadsheets/SKILL.md)
### How to use skills
- Discovery: The list above is the skills available in this session (name + description + file path). Skill bodies live on disk at the listed paths.
- Trigger rules: If the user names a skill (with `$SkillName` or plain text) OR the task clearly matches a skill's description shown above, you must use that skill for that turn. Multiple mentions mean use them all. Do not carry skills across turns unless re-mentioned.
- Missing/blocked: If a named skill isn't in the list or the path can't be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.
- How to use a skill (progressive disclosure):
  1) After deciding to use a skill, open its `SKILL.md`. Read only enough to follow the workflow.
  2) When `SKILL.md` references relative paths (e.g., `scripts/foo.py`), resolve them relative to the skill directory listed above first, and only consider other paths if needed.
  3) If `SKILL.md` points to extra folders such as `references/`, load only the specific files needed for the request; don't bulk-load everything.
  4) If `scripts/` exist, prefer running or patching them instead of retyping large code blocks.
  5) If `assets/` or templates exist, reuse them instead of recreating from scratch.
- Coordination and sequencing:
  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.
  - Announce which skill(s) you're using and why (one short line). If you skip an obvious skill, say why.
- Context hygiene:
  - Keep context small: summarize long sections instead of pasting them; only load extra files when needed.
  - Avoid deep reference-chasing: prefer opening only files directly linked from `SKILL.md` unless you're blocked.
  - When variants exist (frameworks, providers, domains), pick only the relevant reference file(s) and note that choice.
- Safety and fallback: If a skill can't be applied cleanly (missing files, unclear instructions), state the issue, pick the next-best approach, and continue.

- `bd update <id> --status=in_progress` - Claim work
- `bd update <id> --assignee=username` - Assign to someone
- `bd update <id> --title/--description/--notes/--design` - Update fields inline
- `bd close <id>` - Mark complete
- `bd close <id1> <id2> ...` - Close multiple issues at once (more efficient)
- `bd close <id> --reason="explanation"` - Close with reason
- **Tip**: When creating multiple issues/tasks/epics, use parallel subagents for efficiency
- **WARNING**: Do NOT use `bd edit` - it opens $EDITOR (vim/nano) which blocks agents

### Dependencies & Blocking
- `bd dep add <issue> <depends-on>` - Add dependency (issue depends on depends-on)
- `bd blocked` - Show all blocked issues
- `bd show <id>` - See what's blocking/blocked by this issue

### Sync & Collaboration
- `bd dolt push` - Push beads to Dolt remote
- `bd dolt pull` - Pull beads from Dolt remote
- `bd search <query>` - Search issues by keyword

### Project Health
- `bd stats` - Project statistics (open/closed/blocked counts)
- `bd doctor` - Check for issues (sync problems, missing hooks)

## Common Workflows

**Starting work:**
```bash
bd ready           # Find available work
bd show <id>       # Review issue details
bd update <id> --status=in_progress  # Claim it
```

**Completing work:**
```bash
bd close <id1> <id2> ...    # Close all completed issues at once
git add . && git commit -m "..."  # Commit code changes
git push                    # Push to remote
```

**Creating dependent work:**
```bash
# Run bd create commands in parallel (use subagents for many items)
bd create --title="Implement feature X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=feature
bd create --title="Write tests for X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task
bd dep add beads-yyy beads-xxx  # Tests depend on Feature (Feature blocks tests)
```

# Scala-to-TypeScript Port Plan

Generated from beads tracker state and project inventory on 2026-03-07.
The authoritative live breakdown lives in the beads database (`bd list --all`).

---

## Goals

1. **Full meaningful Scala coverage** — achieve effective 100% line/branch coverage
   on all portable business logic. Coverage must be meaningful (actual assertions, not
   just execution). Scoverage is the measurement tool; Codacy is the gate.

2. **Portable contract layer** — define JSON Schema-backed shared fixtures at every
   core/api seam. Scala generates and validates fixtures; TypeScript consumes and
   validates them. The schema is the source of truth, not either language's types.

3. **Incremental TypeScript replacement** — replace the Scala backend one component at
   a time, starting with the scheduler. Each component goes live only after Scala
   coverage is solid, portable fixtures are published, and TypeScript parity tests pass.

---

## Scope Exclusions

- **Spark / analytics models** — `ss.models.analysis`, `ss.models.events.pipeline`
  and all `java.sql.Timestamp`-based types stay JVM-only and are excluded from the
  portable contract backlog.
- **Runtime config DTOs** — `ss.config.main.*` (Kafka, Dragonfly, ClickHouse, workers)
  are Scala composition-root concerns; they are not cross-language domain targets.
- **Akka message types** — `AkkaMessage.scala` and associated actor-routing types are
  not ported.
- **`core/api/system`** — `Worker`, `TDataSource`, `TQueue` are runtime seams, not
  business-domain ports. They stay Scala-only until Stage 6.

---

## Operating Rules

- **Scala coverage first.** No component moves to TypeScript porting until its Scala
  coverage meets the per-component threshold.
- **Fixtures as contract.** Every ported component must have Scala fixture generators
  and golden-file validation before TypeScript contract tests are written.
- **Onion discipline.** Domain and application layers must not import infrastructure or
  transport packages. CI enforces this via boundary checks (Stage 8).
- **One commit per bead.** Stage only files touched for a given bead iteration;
  close the bead only after checks pass.
- **`sbt fmt` before every Scala commit.** CI rejects unformatted code.

---

## Technology Decisions

### Observability Stack

- **Tracing:** OpenTelemetry (OTEL). Scala side uses the existing tracing helpers.
  TypeScript side uses `@opentelemetry/sdk-node` with equivalent span propagation.
- **Logging:** Structured JSON (ZIO Logging on Scala; `pino` or equivalent on TypeScript).
  Log field names and context keys must match across languages for collector compatibility.
- **Metrics:** Prometheus-compatible exposition. Scala uses existing ZIO Metrics setup.
  TypeScript exposes the same metric names via OTEL metrics or a compatible exporter.
- **Context propagation:** W3C `traceparent`/`tracestate` headers at all service boundaries.

### TypeScript Runtime

- **Effect-TS** (`effect`) for typed dependency injection, structured concurrency, and
  error modeling. Services, adapters, and transports compose through explicit `Layer`
  definitions in a composition root.
- **Vitest** for unit, contract, and parity tests.
- **`tsc --noEmit`** (`typecheck` script) for type validation in CI.
- **pnpm workspaces** for the `packages/` monorepo.

### Infrastructure

- **Redis/Dragonfly** — scheduler persistence adapter uses ioredis; tested via
  Testcontainers in integration suites.
- **PostgreSQL** — job and profile adapters; Testcontainers for integration tests.
- **JSON Schema 2020-12** — canonical wire format for fixtures. Ajv (TypeScript) and
  `com.networknt:json-schema-validator` (Scala) validate against the same schema files.

---

## Package Layout

```
packages/
  scheduler/          # Stage 1 pilot — scheduler and slotting
    src/
      domain/         # Shared domain types (ids, profile, scheduler-target)
      algorithms/     # Pure scheduling logic
      slotting/       # Slot calculation and seam
      models/         # Scheduler model types
      adapters/       # Redis/persistence adapters
      distribution/   # Distribution logic
      filter/         # Filter helpers
      persistence/    # Persistence port implementations
      profile/        # Profile helpers
      scheduler.ts    # Package entry point
    tests/
      unit/           # Pure logic tests
      contracts/      # Fixture-driven contract tests
      parity/         # Scala output parity validation
      integration/    # Testcontainers-backed adapter tests
      adapters/       # Adapter-specific suites
```

Future packages follow the same layout pattern for each ported component.

---

## Wire Format and Fixture Schema Ownership

```
fixtures/
  README.md
  schemas/
    README.md
    <component>/
      <type>.schema.json        # JSON Schema 2020-12; $id rooted under fixtures/
  <component>/
    <scenario>.json             # Generated and checked-in fixture JSON
```

- **Scala generators own fixture production.** TypeScript consumes but does not generate.
- **Schema is the source of truth.** Both sides validate against schema before asserting.
- **`$id` must match the checked-in path** so sibling `$ref`s resolve locally without
  network fetches (Ajv pre-registration by `$id`; Scala uses local file mapping).
- **Fixture names are scenario-oriented** (e.g. `force-scheduler.json`); schema names
  are type-oriented (e.g. `schedule-batch-fixture.schema.json`).
- **Transitional:** Scheduler parity fixtures currently live under
  `packages/scheduler/tests/parity/fixtures/`. New work targets `fixtures/` root.

---

## Runtime Coexistence Strategy

During the port, Scala and TypeScript services run side-by-side:

1. Scala remains the production runtime until a component's TypeScript replacement
   passes all parity tests in CI.
2. Feature flags gate traffic routing to TypeScript implementations.
3. A ported component is promoted to production only after:
   - Its Scala coverage target is met.
   - Fixture golden files are stable and checked in.
   - TypeScript parity tests pass on fixture data.
   - O11y parity checklist (foj.8.3) is satisfied for that component.

---

## Coverage Definitions

- **Meaningful coverage**: every covered line must have at least one assertion about
  observable behavior (output, exception, state transition). Pure execution without
  assertions does not count.
- **Scoverage** (statement + branch) is the Scala measurement tool.
- **@vitest/coverage-v8** is the TypeScript measurement tool.
- **Thresholds** are enforced in CI. Drops below per-component baselines block merge.
- **Scoverage baseline**: established after Stage 0 cleanup completes. Each stage
  defines its own target before TypeScript porting begins.

# Backend Interface Plan

## Goal

Portability requires three things at the same time:

1. Each backend component must expose a stable interface boundary.
2. The behavior behind that boundary must be testable without the full application shell.
3. The same behavioral contract must run against the Scala implementation and any alternate implementation.

The source of truth for existing backend ports is `core/api/src/main/scala/ss/api`.

## Component Map

### 1. Core domain and shared contracts

- Scope: `core/models`, `core/api`, `core/utils`
- Current interfaces:
  - Domain models and codecs in `core/models`
  - Cross-module service ports in `core/api`
  - Shared ZIO/tracing helpers in `core/utils`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Keep `core/models` pure and dependency-light.
  - Treat `core/api` as the only allowed cross-module dependency surface.
  - Remove direct module-to-module implementation coupling where code bypasses `core/api`.
  - Split overly broad `T*Service` traits into read/write or orchestration/kernel ports where needed.
- Portable tests:
  - Serialization and codec contract tests.
  - Port contract suites with in-memory fakes.
  - Model-level golden fixtures for cross-language parity.

### 2. Accounts and authorization

- Scope: `modules/accounts`, `core/api/accounts`
- Current interfaces:
  - Account lifecycle: `TAccountService`, `TAccountsPersistence`
  - Authorization and auth context: `TAccountAuthorizationService`, `TAuthorizingContextService`, `TUserAccountsContextProvider`
  - Tokens and auth providers: `TAuthTokenService`, `TTokenAuthService`, `TAuth0Client`
  - Feature flags: `TFeatureFlagsService`
  - Billing/subscription edges: `TSubscriptionService`, `TAccountAuditLogService`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Separate identity/authn, authorization, feature flags, and subscription logic into distinct service seams.
  - Replace mixed persistence-and-policy services with a pure policy layer over repository ports.
  - Normalize mock support so every account-facing service can run with in-memory adapters.
- Portable tests:
  - Authorization decision tables.
  - Token issuance/validation contract suite.
  - Feature-flag fallback behavior contract.
  - Subscription state transition contract.

### 3. Profiles and contact graph

- Scope: `modules/profiles`, `core/api/profiles`
- Current interfaces:
  - Contact read/write: `TContactsPersistence`, `TContactsService`, `TContactsServiceV2`, `TContactsSyncServiceV2`
  - Profile lookup: `TProfilesPersistence`, `TContactProfilesService`, `TContactProfilesServiceV2`
  - Profile properties: `TProfilesPropertiesPersistence`, `TProfilesPropertiesService`, `TProfilesPropertiesSyncService`
  - Ancillary UI/API services: `TProfileWidgetsService`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Collapse legacy/v2 duplication behind a single canonical profile/contact contract.
  - Split synchronization from lookup APIs.
  - Move profile computation kernels into pure functions where they are still embedded in service orchestration.
- Portable tests:
  - Contact sync contract using deterministic contact fixtures.
  - Profile lookup contract over in-memory persistence.
  - Profile-properties sync contract over ClickHouse/Kafka stubs.

### 4. Lists and scheduler

- Scope: `modules/lists`, `core/api/profiles/TSchedulerService.scala`, `core/api/scheduler`
- Current interfaces:
  - Batch scheduling: `TSchedulerService`
  - Slotting: `TSlottingPersistence`, `TSlottingService`
  - Direct action scheduling flow: `TDirectActionScheduler`, `TDirectActionSchedulerFactory`, `TDirectActionTargetLoader`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Separate pure scheduling kernel from profile/contact loading orchestration.
  - Keep slotting as an adapter port, not embedded in algorithm logic.
  - Standardize serialized fixtures for schedule params, inputs, outputs, and state.
- Portable tests:
  - Deterministic algorithm contract tests.
  - Multi-batch state-carryover contract tests.
  - Statistical parity tests for randomized schedulers.
  - Adapter compliance tests for slotting persistence.
- Status:
  - First contract extraction is now implemented in `packages/scheduler/tests/contracts`.

### 5. Actions and callback workflows

- Scope: `modules/actions`, `core/api/actions`
- Current interfaces:
  - Scheduling: `TCallbackActionScheduler`, `TCallbackJobScheduler`
  - Execution: `TCallbackJobExecutor`
  - Queue/persistence: `TCallbackActionsQueue`, `TCallbackJobsPersistence`, `TCallbackQueuedActionsPersistence`, `TCallbackScheduledActionsPersistence`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Split workflow orchestration from delivery/execution side effects.
  - Extract callback job state transitions into a pure state machine.
  - Replace mixed cache/persistence implementations with adapter wrappers behind a single port.
- Portable tests:
  - Callback job scheduling contract.
  - Callback executor idempotency contract.
  - Queue and persistence adapter suites using in-memory backends first.

### 6. Jobs and job-state orchestration

- Scope: `modules/jobs`, `core/api/jobs`, `core/api/scheduler/TJobState*`
- Current interfaces:
  - Job lifecycle: `TJobService`, `TJobInitiatorService`
  - Progress/stats: `TJobProgressService`, `TJobStatsService`
  - Persistence/queue: `TJobsPersistence`, `TJobsQueue`
  - Scheduled actions: `TScheduledActionsPersistence`, `TScheduledActionsService`, `TScheduledActionCreator`, `TScheduledActionArchiving`
  - State processing: `TJobStateProcessor`, `TJobStateProducer`, `TJobStateServicesFactory`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Isolate job-state transitions from worker/runtime concerns.
  - Split queue-triggering behavior from persistence mutations.
  - Make scheduled-action creation a pure planning step plus side-effect adapters.
- Portable tests:
  - Job state transition contracts.
  - Scheduled action planning contracts.
  - Queue integration adapter tests.

### 7. Connectors and content

- Scope: `modules/connectors`, `core/api/connectors`, `core/api/content`
- Current interfaces:
  - Connector management: `TConnectorService`, `TConnectorsPersistence`, `TConnectorScopesPersistence`
  - Connector execution: `TConnectorClient`, `TConnectorClientFactory`, `TCRMObjectClient`, `TConnectorEventsLoader`
  - Connector queueing: `TConnectorsQueue`
  - Content: `TContentService`, `TContentsPersistence`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Split connector metadata management from connector-runtime clients.
  - Standardize connector client capabilities so providers implement a smaller, more explicit subset.
  - Move `TContentService` ownership fully into the connectors domain or create a dedicated content module.
- Portable tests:
  - Connector client capability contracts.
  - Content service contract.
  - Queue and persistence adapter suites.

### 8. Events enrichment and analytics ingest

- Scope: `modules/events`, `core/api/events`
- Current interfaces:
  - Chunk persistence: `TEventsChunksPersistence`, `TEventsChunksStatsPersistence`
  - Enrichment pipeline: `TEventsEnrichmentService`, `TEventsProcessingService`
  - Support services: `TGeocodingService`, `TInboxProviderService`, `TEmailCampaignsPersistence`, `TEventsArchive`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Treat event enrichment stages as explicit pipelines with typed input/output contracts.
  - Extract stage-local pure transforms from persistence and third-party calls.
  - Make archive and chunk persistence pluggable adapters.
- Portable tests:
  - Stage 1 -> Stage 2 pipeline contracts.
  - Enrichment service fixture tests.
  - ClickHouse/archive adapter tests.

### 9. Emails and notifications

- Scope: `modules/emails`, `core/api/emails`
- Current interfaces:
  - Mail delivery: `TEmailService`
  - Notification edges: `TAccountEmailNotifier`, `TSubscriptionEmailNotifier`
  - Job progress publication: reused `TJobProgressService`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Separate template/rendering behavior from transport.
  - Make notification composition deterministic and testable without SMTP.
- Portable tests:
  - Notification rendering contract.
  - Delivery transport contract using fake mail adapters.

### 10. Subscription integrations

- Scope: `integrations/recurly`, `core/api/subscription`, account subscription services
- Current interfaces:
  - External billing client: `TExternalSubscriptionsClient`
  - Internal persistence: `TSubscriptionsPersistence`
  - Recurly-specific support: `TRecurlySyncSubscriptionService`, `TRecurlySignatureService`
- Cleanup plan:
  - Keep provider-specific webhook/signature logic inside integration packages.
  - Expose provider-neutral subscription events/state transitions to the rest of the system.
- Portable tests:
  - External subscription client contract.
  - Webhook signature verification contract.
  - Subscription sync contract with recorded fixtures.

### 11. Provider-specific integrations

- Scope: `integrations/cloudflare`, `integrations/hubspot/*`, `integrations/marketo-ssfs`
- Current interfaces:
  - Cloudflare: DNS, geocoding, inbox-provider ports
  - HubSpot: cards, actions, signatures, content, CRM object access
  - Marketo SSFS: auth, flow-step callback scheduling/execution
- Cleanup plan:
  - Limit provider packages to adapter implementations and provider-specific workflow glue.
  - Move reusable business rules back into module-level ports.
  - Standardize recorded-fixture testing for external APIs.
- Portable tests:
  - Adapter conformance suites per provider capability.
  - Fixture-driven request/response contracts.

### 12. Infrastructure adapters

- Scope: `infrastructure/postgres`, `infrastructure/kafka`, `infrastructure/clickhouse`, `infrastructure/dragonfly`
- Current interfaces:
  - Postgres: most `*Persistence` and queue implementations
  - Kafka/Redpanda: queue and dead-letter implementations, profile property sync
  - ClickHouse: analytics persistence
  - Dragonfly: slotting persistence
- Cleanup plan:
  - Treat each adapter package as replaceable infrastructure only.
  - Add adapter test suites that every implementation must pass.
  - Keep serialization schemas centralized so alternate implementations can share fixtures.
- Portable tests:
  - Repository contract tests.
  - Queue semantics contract tests.
  - Slotting persistence adapter contract tests.

### 13. Application composition and transport

- Scope: `omnibus`, `modules/akka`, `interfaces/tapir`, `interfaces/caliban`, `interfaces/graphile`
- Current interfaces:
  - Wiring/composition in `omnibus`
  - Worker/runtime orchestration in `modules/akka`
  - HTTP/GraphQL transport in interface packages
- Cleanup plan:
  - Keep transport thin; all meaningful behavior belongs behind module ports.
  - Make workers call port interfaces only, not concrete implementations.
  - Push logic out of routers and request handlers into testable services.
- Portable tests:
  - Transport contract tests against fake services.
  - End-to-end smoke tests only after port contracts exist.

## Cleanup Sequence

1. Lock `core/api` as the canonical port surface.
2. For each component, split pure decision logic from orchestration and side effects.
3. Add a contract test suite for the component port.
4. Provide one in-memory or fixture-backed adapter for the contract suite.
5. Run the same suite against the Scala implementation.
6. Port the component to TypeScript or another target and run the same suite there.
7. Only after the contract passes in both places, switch callers over.

## Recommended Order

1. Lists/scheduler
2. Slotting
3. Actions/callback scheduling
4. Jobs/job-state services
5. Profiles/contact services
6. Accounts/auth/feature flags
7. Connectors/content
8. Events enrichment
9. Subscription and provider integrations
10. Transport layers

This order follows the current codebase reality: scheduler and slotting already have a partial TypeScript port and parity fixtures, so they are the fastest place to harden the process before moving into more stateful modules.

## Observability Acceptance Criterion

A ported TypeScript service satisfies the O11y parity requirement when:

1. **Traces**: Every inbound request opens a span; outbound calls to adapters and
   external services create child spans. `traceparent` is propagated via W3C headers.
   Span names match the Scala equivalent operation names.

2. **Structured logging**: Log entries are JSON. Required fields match the Scala
   equivalents: `timestamp`, `level`, `message`, `traceId`, `spanId`, and any
   domain-specific annotation fields (e.g. `accountId`, `jobId`).

3. **Metrics**: The same metric names and label cardinality as the Scala implementation.
   Counter and histogram semantics preserved. Prometheus-compatible exposition.

4. **Context rehydration**: For worker-style services, span context must be rehydrated
   from stored trace context on job dequeue. A test fixture exercises round-trip
   rehydration.

Acceptance is verified by the O11y parity checklist (foj.8.3) before any TS
component is promoted to production.
